question: ATS 7.10.1.D.2 on current transformers requires polarity results to:
choices: Be within 2% of the adjacent phase
Be ignored if the ratio is within 5%
explanation: Polarity agrees with the marks. A ratio can look plausible while H1/X1 are reversed, and a reversed CT in a differential scheme looks like an internal fault as soon as load flows.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.D.2

question: How many grounding points does ATS 7.10.1 allow on a CT secondary circuit?
choices: Exactly one, at the location the drawings specify
One at each end of the run
One per phase plus one on the neutral
explanation: The secondary circuit is grounded, and it has only one grounding point, located where the engineer showed it, consistent with IEEE C57.13.3. A second ground circulates current. No ground lets the circuit float.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.B.9 and D.9

question: ATS 7.10.2.D.3 ratio-error limits for voltage transformers are:
choices: ±0.1% for revenue metering; the other-applications sentence states +1.2% ratio and ±17.5 mrad phase angle
No numeric limit; only polarity is checked
explanation: Revenue metering is ±0.1% ratio and ±0.9 mrad. Other applications are written as not exceeding +1.2% ratio and ±17.5 mrad (one degree). A ±3% field screen from a VT manufacturer bulletin is a different test, done at very low voltage, and is not this paragraph.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.2.D.3

question: Insulation resistance of a current transformer and its secondary wiring, ATS 7.10.1, is:
choices: 1000 V DC for one minute, unless solid-state parts cannot take it
A megger is forbidden on CT wiring
explanation: 7.10.1.B.1 specifies 1000 V DC for one minute on each CT and its secondary wiring to ground. If a device on that wiring cannot survive the voltage, follow the manufacturer instead of forcing the shot.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.B.1

question: ATS 7.10.1 requires an excitation test on which CTs?
choices: Every window CT, and never a bushing CT
None; excitation was removed from the section
explanation: ATS 7.10.1.B.4 calls for an excitation test on relaying current transformers, done in accordance with IEEE C57.13.1. Clause 6.5 of that guide says the test checks the accuracy rating and looks for shorted turns, against the manufacturer’s curve. Metering CTs still get ratio and polarity.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.B.4 and D.4; ref. IEEE C57.13.1-2017, clause 6.5

question: Burden of a CT circuit is measured:
choices: At the shorting block, with the secondary open under load
At the CT shorting terminal block, per IEEE C57.13.1
explanation: ATS 7.10.1.B.5 measures the current-circuit burden at the CT shorting block, in accordance with IEEE C57.13.1. Clause 6.7 says that check is made with secondary current flowing, preferably near rated current, into a known burden. Extra lead and extra relays are what push the CT toward saturation.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.B.5; ref. IEEE C57.13.1-2017, clause 6.7

question: Ratio of a CT, ATS 7.10.1, is verified by:
choices: The voltage or current method in IEEE C57.13.1
explanation: ATS 7.10.1.B.3 names the voltage method or the current method, both under IEEE C57.13.1. Those methods are in clause 8. Polarity, clause 9, still has to agree with the marks. A ratio that matches the nameplate with the marks reversed is a failed polarity test.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.B.3 and D.2; ref. IEEE C57.13.1-2017, clauses 8 and 9

question: You finished a CT with a DC resistance reading and skipped excitation. The core is:
choices: Demagnetized, because DC resistance is gentle
Likely left magnetized; excitation is what works the flux back down
Required to be hipot tested next
explanation: A DC resistance reading can leave the core magnetized. To demagnetize it, use the excitation hookup, raise the AC voltage past saturation, and then lower that voltage slowly and continuously all the way to zero. Reaching saturation and stopping there does not take the magnetism out. ATS-2025 7.10.1.B.4 still requires the excitation test on relaying CTs.

question: IEEE 30°, IEEE 45°, and the 10/50 knee are:
choices: Different markers on the excitation curve
explanation: The three names are different points people mark on one excitation plot. IEEE C57.13.1-2017 clauses 6.5 and 12 tell you to compare the curve with the manufacturer's curve and to take readings near the knee. They do not define a 30-degree knee, a 45-degree knee, or a 10/50 knee. Say which marker you used.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.D.4; IEEE C57.13.1-2017, clauses 6.5 and 12

question: A potential-transformer check includes polarity. Valence’s PT/VT back-to-basics list, and ATS 7.10.2, both treat a wrong polarity as:
choices: Acceptable if the ratio is close
A failed test; the marks have to agree
Fixed by changing the fuse size
Only a metering problem, not a relay problem
explanation: Polarity has to match the marks. A reversed VT in a directional or synchronizing scheme is a wrong torque or a wrong close. Ratio alone does not catch it. Credit: Valence, potential transformer testing.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.2.D.2; Valence, Potential transformer testing

question: Valence’s PT/VT checklist calls out primary and secondary fuse sizes because:
choices: Any fuse that fits is fine
A wrong fuse can open on a normal burden or fail to clear a faulted secondary
explanation: The fuse has to match the VT and the burden. Too small and it opens in service; too large and a shorted secondary is not cleared. That check is visual against the drawings, then the ratio and polarity tests still happen. Credit: Valence.
reference: Valence, Potential transformer testing; ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.2 includes fuse verification in the inspection

question: Turns ratio on a tapped VT, when the taps are accessible, is performed:
choices: On all tap positions you can reach
Only if the fuse is blown
explanation: ATS 7.10.2 calls for a turns-ratio test on all tap positions. A bad tap will not show on the tap you happened to find in service. Valence’s list says the same thing.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.2.B.3; Valence, Potential transformer testing

question: A low-voltage turns-ratio check on a PT proves:
choices: The nameplate accuracy class at full voltage and full burden
That the ratio and polarity are in the right neighborhood for the marks, not the revenue accuracy
explanation: A handheld TTR applies a small voltage. It will catch a wrong tap or a reversed winding. It will not reproduce the factory accuracy test at 90, 100, and 110 percent voltage. ATS 7.10.2 still requires the ratio and the polarity check.
reference: Valence, Potential transformer testing; ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.2

question: VT secondary burden is measured so you can see whether:
choices: The connected relays and cable exceed what the VT was rated to drive
The primary fuse is the right class
explanation: Burden is the load on the secondary. Too much and the VT sags and the relay or meter sees the wrong voltage. ATS 7.10.2 includes measuring the voltage-circuit burden at the transformer terminals and comparing it with the rating.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.2

question: ATS 7.10.1.B.1 insulation-resistance test on a current transformer and its secondary wiring is:
choices: 1000 V dc for one minute, unless solid-state parts cannot take that voltage
A power-factor test at 10 kV only
explanation: Each CT and its secondary wiring is tested to ground at 1000 V dc for one minute. If solid-state parts cannot tolerate that, follow the manufacturer. The minimum resistance is Table 100.5, not a guess.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.B.1 and D.1

question: ATS 7.10.1.B.4 requires an excitation test:
choices: On every metering CT and never on a relaying CT
On current transformers used for relaying, in accordance with IEEE C57.13.1
Only if the ratio already failed
With the primary left connected to the bus
explanation: Relaying CTs get the excitation test. IEEE C57.13.1-2017 clause 6.5 compares the result with the manufacturer’s curve and uses it to find shorted turns. Clause 12 is how the test is run. Metering CTs still get ratio and polarity.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.B.4 and D.4; ref. IEEE C57.13.1-2017, clauses 6.5 and 12

question: ATS 7.1.1.A.7 says the current and voltage transformer ratios in switchgear must:
choices: Be the highest ratio in the catalog
Be ignored if the relay is microprocessor
explanation: A CT ratio that is not the ratio on the drawing makes every relay setting wrong in primary amperes. The check is visual against the nameplate and the drawing, before the electrical tests in 7.10.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.1.1.A.7

question: Instrument transformers mounted on a liquid-filled power transformer are tested by ATS 7.2.2.B.16:
choices: With the transformer turns-ratio set only
Not at all, if the nameplate ratio is printed
explanation: Bushing CTs and other instrument transformers get the 7.10 tests: insulation resistance, polarity, ratio, and, for relaying CTs, excitation. The power-transformer ratio test does not cover them.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.2.2.B.16 and D.16

question: IEEE C57.13.1-2017 clause 6.5 says an excitation test is used to confirm that a relaying CT:
choices: Matches its accuracy class and has no shorted turns, against the manufacturer’s curve
explanation: Shorted turns and a wiring fault show up as a curve that is not the one the manufacturer drew. ATS 7.10.1.B.4 requires the test on relaying CTs and 7.10.1.D.4 compares it with that curve or with this guide.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.B.4 and D.4; ref. IEEE C57.13.1-2017, clause 6.5

question: The voltage method in IEEE C57.13.1-2017 clause 12.2.1 is run by:
choices: Applying AC to the secondary with the primary open, after demagnetizing
Applying DC to the primary while the secondary is shorted
Leaving the CT on the live bus
explanation: This is the usual field method because it does not need a high-current set. Clause 12.2.1 says to demagnetize first (see 5.1). The primary stays open. ATS 7.10.1.B.4 is the test that uses this method.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.B.4; ref. IEEE C57.13.1-2017, clauses 5.1 and 12.2.1

question: IEEE C57.13.1-2017 clause 6.7 allows a CT burden test only when:
choices: Secondary current is flowing, preferably near rated current
The CT is above the knee for 10 minutes
explanation: The test asks whether the CT can push a known current, set by its ratio, into a known burden and still hold its accuracy. ATS 7.10.1.B.5 measures that burden at the shorting block. An open secondary is not this test.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.B.5; ref. IEEE C57.13.1-2017, clause 6.7

question: On the DC polarity check in IEEE C57.13.1-2017 clause 9.1, correct marks give a meter that:
choices: Kicks upscale when the battery is connected and downscale when it is opened
Kicks downscale on connection if X1 is positive
explanation: A small DC source is touched to the secondary and an analog meter watches the primary mark. Upscale on connect and downscale on release means the marks agree, for the hookup in that clause. ATS 7.10.1.D.2 fails the CT if the polarity does not match the marks. Clause 9 also allows AC and current methods.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.B.2 and D.2; ref. IEEE C57.13.1-2017, clause 9.1

question: For an excitation test, IEEE C57.13.1-2017 clause 12.2 wants the ammeter to be rms and the voltmeter to be:
choices: Average-responding, scaled to match an rms meter on a sine wave
explanation: The winding is nonlinear, so the voltage wave is not a clean sine. An average-responding meter, with bandwidth through the third harmonic, keeps the voltage reading from chasing those harmonics. ATS 7.10.1.D.4 still compares the curve you plot with the manufacturer’s curve.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.D.4; ref. IEEE C57.13.1-2017, clause 12.2

question: IEEE C57.13.1-2017 clause 12.2.1 says the points that matter most when you plot an excitation curve are:
explanation: The knee is where the curve leaves the straight part. A plot that stops early cannot be compared with the manufacturer’s curve. Clause 6.5 is why ATS 7.10.1 asks for that comparison on a relaying CT.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.D.4; ref. IEEE C57.13.1-2017, clause 12.2.1

question: IEEE C57.13.1-2017 clause 6.4 uses a DC resistance measurement on a CT secondary to find:
choices: A high-resistance joint in the winding or the connected wiring
explanation: The resistance should match the specification, and the test is also looking for a bad connection. It is not the excitation test and it is not polarity. ATS 7.10.1 still requires the ratio, polarity, and, for relaying CTs, the excitation test in the same guide.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1; ref. IEEE C57.13.1-2017, clause 6.4

question: A bar-type CT, as ATS 7.10.1 uses the term, has:
choices: No primary of its own; only a window
A primary bar that is part of the transformer
A split core that opens after the cable is made up
A secondary that is never grounded
explanation: The section tests the primary of a bar-type CT with the secondary grounded. The bar is the primary. A window CT has to have the cable pass through the opening, so it is placed before that cable is terminated. ATS does not give a separate procedure named split-core.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.B.6

question: The temperature-rise rating of a CT is taken from:
choices: The CT nameplate, checked against the drawings
explanation: ATS 7.10.1 starts by comparing the nameplate with the drawings. That is where the ratings, including temperature rise, are read. Table 100.18, the relay tap, and a microhmmeter do not set that rating.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.A.1

question: A CT that can be opened and placed around a cable that is already terminated is commonly called:
explanation: A split-core CT opens on a hinge or joint so it can go around a conductor that is already terminated. A solid window CT needs that conductor threaded through the opening before the termination is made. ATS-2025 7.10.1.B.6 and B.7 name bar-type CTs for the primary insulation-resistance and withstand tests. They do not define the split-core name, and they do not tell you the cable must pass through a window as a contrast with a bar-type unit.
reference: Engineering fundamentals (split-core CT); ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.10.1.B.6 and B.7
